title: Regulatory effects of Maillard reaction precursors on humification during co-composting of spent mushroom substrate and pig manure at extreme mixing ratios
content:
by Ming Sun, Yanyan Liu, Baoyi Lu, Mingshuo Wang, Pingxin Liu

Spent mushroom substrate (SMS) and pig manure (PM) represent two dominant types of agricultural organic waste. Co-composting of these two substrates at extreme mixing ratios—common in regions with a surplus of a single waste type—frequently suffers from C/N imbalance, suppressed humification, and substantial nutrient loss. Maillard reaction precursors (MRPs) are well-documented key regulators of humus (HS) formation, yet their regulatory mechanisms and efficacy in SMS–PM co-composting at extreme mixing ratios remain poorly understood. In this study, we performed a 120-day aerobic solid-state incubation experiment using two extreme SMS: PM mass ratios (9:1 for the high-SMS system, 1:9 for the high-PM system), with catechol (Cat), glucose (Glu), and glycine (Gly) applied as exogenous MRPs. The results demonstrated that all three MRPs significantly improved compost maturity, nutrient retention, and HS synthesis relative to the unamended control. Glu accelerated phytotoxin degradation, increased GI by 26.8%–45.7%, and HIX by 66.7%–276.4%, and adapted well to high-PM systems by promoting humic acid (HA) synthesis and polymerization. Gly yielded the optimal nitrogen (N) fixation effect (total N increased by 18.7%–29.4%) and alleviated HA degradation in high-SMS systems. Cat reduced salinity via ion chelation but exhibited a slower humification rate. PLS-SEM analysis revealed that MRPs directly promoted humification in high-SMS systems, while indirectly regulating humification by optimizing biochemical properties in high-PM systems. FTIR spectroscopy and elemental analysis confirmed that MRPs enhanced the aromatization degree and molecular stability of HA. These findings clarify the substrate-ratio-dependent regulatory effects of MRPs on compost humification during solid-state aerobic incubation mimicking co-composting conditions and provide targeted strategies for the sustainable high-value utilization of agricultural organic wastes.
